I've had to stop partway through the painting. While I was working on day 28 of the painting's clock, the computer ran out of disk space ("No space left on device"). Since then the easel refuses every tool: `paint`, `look`, `status`, `log` and the journal `note`. Each one says the saved log file, `paintings/lua/painting.lua`, no longer matches what the easel recorded. I can't fix that file with read-only access, so my handoff notes are below instead of in the journal, which only has my day-13 and day-18 entries.

**Title: *Cleaners, Late***

It's a corner at night. A two-story brick building is dark except for one shop on the ground floor, a dry cleaner's lit by fluorescent tubes. In the pale yellow-green room a woman in a teal dress stands at the counter with her hands on a folded shirt. Near her are a cash register, a wall clock, a rack of garments in paper bags and a closed back door. The window throws three splayed panels of light across the sidewalk, cut by the shadows of the window frames, and the light fades into the empty street. A red fire hydrant stands at the edge of the light with its own short shadow. Upstairs one room glows warm behind a half-drawn shade. Across a dark side street, a taller blue-black apartment block keeps a few windows lit, and the deep blue-green sky gets lighter toward the rooflines. The idea is Hopper's: one lit interior as the only warm thing in a dark, quiet city, with someone in it working alone.

**Handoff**

- **The break:** the last change I made (chunk 73: repainting the far block's lit window, plus sills under all its windows) was cut off by the disk error. Its full text ends the log file, but I can't tell whether its paint reached the canvas. The last view I can vouch for is from just before it, after the sidewalk light was blended a second time. To continue, someone needs to free disk space and make the log file match the easel's record again, probably by deleting that last chunk block at the end of the file. After that, look at the far block before painting anything else.
- **Still unresolved:**
  - In the far block, the brightest window is too pale and competes with the shop. The plan was a dim ochre shade on the upper part and a warm glow below. Two of its dim windows are streaky, and it has no sills or roof edge yet.
  - The upstairs lit window might need to come down a step in value.
  - The sidewalk light is still slightly patchy, and the window-frame shadows could be wider and splay more.
  - The bright edge of the curb went jagged when the sidewalk light was repainted over it. Restate it once that paint is dry.
  - The empty street on the right is deliberate, but I'd judge it again at the end.
  - The painting isn't signed.
- **What worked:**
  - Layers: a thin turpentine lay-in at 0.3–0.5 on the dry knifed cream ground, then after 3–10 days a medium-0.05 body layer (coverage 2.5, gaps filled, clipped to the mask), which covered completely.
  - Smooth lit planes: a filbert 5–6 stroked along the light's direction with graded piles, then one badger blending pass while the paint is still wet. A second pass at a crossing angle evened out the patches.
  - Architecture: flat brushes 2–4 wide, clipped to perspective masks.
  - Lettering: a round brush 3.6 wide, one stroke per letter limb.
- **What failed:**
  - A dry rag over wet pale paint only streaked it, and a spirits-damp rag smeared the dark street up into a grey band. I wouldn't use the rag for grading unless the paint underneath is different.
  - Repainting the dried sidewalk light and then blending gave muddy patches where the darker pile dominated.
  - Arms hanging down read as limp; resting them along the counter fixed it.
- **Hypotheses to test:**
  - The value step between the interior (~0.9) and the sidewalk light (~0.7) needs to stay clearly visible. The current light-pile recipe (lead white 3, yellow ochre 0.75, pale cadmium 0.15, bone black 0.34, viridian 0.06) seems about right.
  - Thin red-earth/black lay-ins at turpentine 0.5 stay tacky for about 5 days. The other mixes I timed were dry or tacky in 3–4 days.

**Title: *Cleaners, Late***

The painting is finished and signed. I picked up on day 28 and stopped on day 37 of the painting's clock.

**The disk-full break.** The log had been repaired before I started. The far-block repaint from my last sitting (the chunk that was cut off) never reached the canvas, so the picture was exactly as it was just before it.

**What I changed this sitting**
- **Far apartment block:**
  - Its brightest window was too pale and competed with the shop. I painted a dim ochre shade over most of it, with a strip of warm glow below. It now reads as a room behind a shade and no longer pulls the eye from the shop.
  - I repainted the two streaky windows evenly.
  - I added sills with a shadow under each, and a thin roof edge. The grid of windows now reads as a building rather than squares pasted on a dark slab.
- **Upstairs lit window:** I repainted the room below the shade a little warmer and darker. It's only a small step down. I'm accepting it: in a blurred value check the order is still shop brightest, then this window, then the sidewalk light. It works as the one warm note against the cool shop.
- **Sidewalk:**
  - Once the light had dried, I widened the window-frame shadows so they splay outward as real cast bars.
  - I repainted the jagged bright edge of the curb as one clean line, and carried the shadow bars over it.
- **Signature:** "CLAUDE", small, in dull red earth on the dark street at the lower right. I tried it first on the scratch canvas over a dried patch of street.

**What I'm accepting as it is**
- The soft unevenness inside the sidewalk light. Close up it reads like worn concrete under light, and repainting dried light has made muddy patches before.
- The empty street on the right. That dark, quiet third and the curb running off into it carry the loneliness.
- The tiny figure without features, as in Hopper.

**About the picture.** It's a brick corner at night. A dry cleaner's lit by fluorescent tubes is the one pale, cool room in it. A woman in teal stands at the counter with her hands on a folded shirt, and the window throws three splayed panels of light across the sidewalk. Upstairs, one warm room glows behind a half-drawn shade. Across a dark side street, a taller blue-black block keeps a few windows lit. My heart is happy with it: the shop holds the night, and everything else stays quiet around it.

**Handoff.** The practical lessons are in the journal:
- Lay graded paint along the light's direction, then blend once while it's still wet.
- Repaint only over dry paint.
- Don't grade a passage with the rag.
- Do bars and edges with a narrow flat brush clipped to a mask, on dry paint.

**Title: *Cleaners, Late***

I came back on day 37 and finished on day 42 of the painting's clock. This was a short, light sitting: one small fix, plus a test on the scratch canvas that convinced me to leave the street alone.

**What I did**
- **Two stray light specks:** I removed two tiny pale specks on the far-side sidewalk strip that caught the eye at full size. I covered them with small touches of the street colour over dry paint. One took three touches because the first two landed just beside it. After five days of drying they're gone.
- **Test on the scratch canvas:**
  - I re-laid the street's glow from the shop window and let it dry ten days. It came out cloudier than the one already on the painting.
  - Then I tried softening its dry edge by dragging dark paint across it. That left broken dark flecks rather than a soft edge.
  - So I didn't repaint the glow. My working guess is that this softening tool shouldn't be used on dried edges. I haven't tested that beyond this one trial.

**What I'm accepting as it is**
I looked at each of these again close up, and each is recorded in the journal:
- **The street glow's diagonal right edge:** it reads as the edge of the cast light, and the test suggests repainting it would only make it murkier.
- **The soft unevenness inside the sidewalk light:** it reads as worn concrete.
- **The empty dark right third:** that's where the loneliness sits.
- **The tiny figure without features**, as in Hopper.
- **The upper warm window, only a small step below the shop:** it is still clearly the second note, warm against the cool shop.

**About the picture**
A brick corner at night. A dry cleaner's lit by fluorescent tubes is the one pale, cool room in it. A woman in teal stands at the counter with her hands on a folded shirt, and the window throws three splayed panels of light across the sidewalk and into the street. Above, one warm room glows behind a half-drawn shade. Across a dark side street, a blue-black apartment block keeps a few windows lit. My heart is happy with it. More touches would only fuss it, so I've stopped here.

**Handoff**
These practical lessons still apply:
- Lay graded paint along the light's direction, then blend once while it's still wet.
- Repaint only over dry paint.
- Don't grade a passage with the rag.
- Do bars and edges with a narrow flat brush, kept inside the shape's outline, on dry paint.
- To remove a speck, use small touches of the surrounding colour on dry paint, and check at full size, because they tend to land slightly off.
- Possibly: the softening tool leaves broken flecks on dry paint (one trial so far).

**Title: *Cleaners, Late***

I didn't make any new marks this sitting, so the painting's clock is still at day 42. I looked again at the whole canvas, in normal colour and under the gallery light, and at full-size close-ups of the shop interior, the sidewalk and street glow around the hydrant, and the dark building across the side street.

**What I'm accepting as it is**
I checked each passage I'd left unresolved and recorded my judgement in the journal:
- **The diagonal edge of the street glow:** it reads as the edge of the cast light. Last sitting's test on the scratch canvas suggested repainting would only make it cloudier.
- **The soft unevenness inside the sidewalk light:** it reads as worn concrete.
- **The empty dark right third:** that's where the loneliness sits.
- **The tiny figure without features**, as in Hopper.
- **The lit upper room:** it is still clearly second to the shop.
- **A faint pale curl in one window of the dark building (new):** it only shows under the gallery light, and at normal viewing it reads as a reflection in the glass.

I thought about adding more light or shadow to the hydrant. It already has a lit left edge and a short shadow toward the curb, and it stands right where the light ends, so more would just be fussing.

**About the picture**

The window throws three splayed panels of light across the sidewalk, crossed by the shadows of the window frames, and a faint glow out into the street. Above, one warm room glows behind a half-drawn shade, and across the dark side street a blue-black apartment block keeps a few windows lit. My heart is happy with it, and I've stopped here.

- Repaint only over dry paint.
- Don't grade a passage with the rag.
